newsitem.title: USA: Dow passes 8,000 mark, bonds rally, dollar tumbles.
newsitem.headline: Dow passes 8,000 mark, bonds rally, dollar tumbles.

text.p: Stocks rallied Wednesday with the Dow Jones industrial average hurdling 8,000 on strong corporate earnings, and mild inflation news sparked a bond rally that took long-term interest rates below 6.5 percent.
The dollar fell amid fear of a potentially troubling Japanese trade report.
The Dow ended up 63.17 points to close at 8,038.88, taking just over five months to rise from the 7,000 level reached on Feb. 13.
The Nasdaq index soared 38.52 points, or 2.50 percent, to 1,580.63, its 10th straight record high and the largest point gain, surpassing the old record of May 2, 1997, when it shot up 35 points.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,990 to 907 on heavy volume of 646 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The other market indices also set new highs.

"It's a powerhouse day for the stock market in general," said Robert Stovall, president of Stovall/21st Advisers. "The Dow is the focus but it's really the junior stocks and the tech stocks that have done so well."
Technology stocks extended their torrid run, and the market was given an extra boost from news that consumer prices rose at their slowest pace in 11 years in the first half of the year.

The Dow's gain came despite a sharp selloff in one of its 30 component stocks, Eastman Kodak Co. Kodak fell 8-3/4 points to 68-1/8 after it reported second-quarter earnings that were well below Wall Street analysts' expectation.
But Kodak's disappointing results were offset by strong earnings elsewhere and further evidence that there are no signs of inflation in the economy.
The Labour Department said the Consumer Price Index, the government's most widely used inflation gauge, rose a smaller-than-expected 0.1 percent in June for the fourth month in a row.

In the inflation-sensitive bond market, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond rose 27/32, lowering its yield to 6.48 percent from 6.55 percent at Tuesday's close. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

"Inflation continues to be tame ... and profits seem to be really good," said Arun Kumar, senior U.S. equities strategist at Lehman Brothers. "So it's a very good recipe for the stock market to perform very well."
Stronger-than-expected earnings reported late Tuesday by semiconductor maker Intel Corp. provided the catalyst for the huge rally in technology shares.
The dollar fell to 1.7910 marks from 1.7935 late Tuesday and to 115.62 Japanese yen from 115.76.
Corn prices fell as forecasts for rain in the Midwest eased fears that recent hot, dry weather would hurt the crop as it enters a key stage of growth this month.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, corn for post-harvest delivery in December closed down 5-3/4 cents a bushel at $2.50-3/4. July corn fell 4-1/4 cents to close at $2.66-1/2.

Soybeans for post-harvest delivery in November fell 16-3/4 cents a bushel to close at $6.09, but the nearby futures contracts dropped even further on talk that a large commercial grain firm may yet deliver cash soybeans against the July contract before it expires on July 22.
July soybeans fell 29 cents to close at $7.82.

In New York, silver futures fell sharply as speculators sold heavily after another government report indicated that inflation remains tame. September silver at the COMEX ended down 11.2 cents at $4.185 an ounce.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 closed at 4,964.2, up 64.9 points, or 1.32 percent. In Tokyo, the 225-stock Nikkei average closed at 20,358.74, up 289.33 points, or 1.44 percent.
